title: Spiritual resistance
hook: secret prayers, hidden schools, Shabbat kept in impossible places

segments.voice: Yesterday, six million, and your line: each one a whole world. Today, what people kept alive inside the walls and the barracks.

Friday night, in a barracks. No table, no white cloth, no wine. Bunks stacked to the ceiling, and everyone exhausted from the day's forced labor. Someone has saved a scrap of bread. Someone else knows the words by heart. In a low voice, almost a whisper, a few people begin to sing the old Shabbat melodies. Others listen from their bunks. Nothing outside has changed. But for a few minutes, inside that room, it is Shabbat. Today's word is what survivors and historians call moments like this.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT IN A BARRACKS.` → `A SCRAP OF BREAD, WORDS BY HEART.` → `FOR A FEW MINUTES, SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Spiritual resistance means refusing to let the enemy decide who you are, even when you cannot stop what they do to you. In the ghettos and the camps, survivors describe it in many forms. Where Jewish schooling was forbidden, teachers held classes in secret, with lookouts at the door and books hidden under coats. People prayed in hiding, sometimes from memory, because the prayer books were gone. Survivors tell of Shabbat candles made from scraps, of tefillin smuggled from hand to hand, of a Passover seder held with no matzah, only the story. There were secret libraries, choirs, lectures and poems. And there were people who could not pray, or chose not to, who kept their dignity in other ways: sharing bread, telling jokes, writing down the truth. Each was a way of saying: you have not made us into what you say we are. In the Warsaw ghetto, a rabbi named Yitzhak Nissenbaum is remembered for a teaching about this. In earlier times of persecution, he said, Jews were asked to sanctify God's name by dying, if they had to, rather than give up their faith. But now the enemy wanted Jewish lives themselves. So the holy task was kiddush ha-chayim, the sanctification of life: to stay alive, and stay human, as an act of faith. The Torah gives one command that turns time itself into something holy: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." No building is needed. No candles, even, if there are none. A day can still be set apart by people who remember it. In impossible places, some of them did.
screen: `REFUSING TO BE WHAT THEY SAY.` · `SECRET CLASSES, PRAYERS BY HEART.` · `THE SANCTIFICATION OF LIFE.` · `A DAY SET APART BY MEMORY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing that keeps you yourself: lighting candles, a blessing before eating, a page, a walk, a song, calling your mother; religious or not. Hold it, and notice how much it means to keep it on purpose. If you pray, let this quiet be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a promise to yourself.

chat.says: If people couldn't fight back, how could they resist at all?
options: By refusing to let the enemy decide who they were: secret classes, prayers, Shabbat.
They couldn't; resistance only means taking up weapons and fighting.
Only those who kept praying resisted; the others simply gave in.
